paras: The threatened lynching of Jack Barnett took place near Catawba Junction, South Carolina, in late November 1888, when parties of men sought to lynch Barnett, a young Black man accused of assaulting a girl. His captors brought him alive to the Yorkville jail, though a later Columbia dispatch said he might be lynched at any moment.

According to a letter from Catawba Junction dated December 3, Barnett met Helen Abernathy and her younger brother and sister on a footpath beside a railroad cut. The correspondent charged that he threw Helen into the cut and attempted to assault her, fleeing when Black women picking cotton nearby answered the children's cries.

Pursuers followed Barnett to Lancaster, where Sep Massey, T. M. Allen and John Lindsay captured him on Thursday morning. He was hurried out of town 'just in time to escape lynching' and brought back to the Junction, where 'another large party' was discussing the same purpose. Crediting the 'law abiding spirit of the Junction people' with restraining that party, the correspondent reported that Massey and J. W. Roddey lodged Barnett in the Yorkville jail that night.
The same letter asserted that the children identified Barnett and that he confessed, a claim found only in the local account. No report of an indictment or trial was found in the coverage.

The Yorkville Enquirer headed the letter 'AN ATROCIOUS OUTRAGE', called Barnett a 'black fiend' and said he 'again escaped his merited punishment', even while praising the Junction's restraint. A Columbia wire ran in the New York Sun on December 9 as 'A Negro in Danger of Lynching' and in the Richmond Daily Times on December 11 as 'WORK OF A NEGRO FIEND', presenting the assault as fact.

The wire said Barnett 'outraged' or 'assaulted' a ten-year-old girl it named 'Aberthney' or 'Bernatheck', and dated the assault to a Thursday evening and, in the Sun, the jailing to December 7. Because the local letter, written on December 3, already described the jailing, its dating of the assault to Wednesday morning is the better evidence.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jack Barnett
bases: Parties gathered to lynch a Black man accused of assaulting a girl while his captors took him to jail; he reached jail alive (A1, A2, A3).

No one was killed: lynching parties followed Barnett and gathered at Catawba Junction over an accusation of assault, but he was lodged in the Yorkville jail (A1, A2, A3), and no later report of his death was found.
The local Yorkville Enquirer letter (A1) and a Columbia wire (A2, A3), which differs in names, ages and dates, agree on the accusation, the capture, the lynching parties and the jailing.

accounts.label: Local correspondent (Catawba Junction, Dec. 3)
accounts.gist: Barnett allegedly tried to assault Helen Abernathy on Wednesday morning, was captured at Lancaster Thursday, hurried away from a lynching there, met another large party at the Junction that was dissuaded, and was jailed at Yorkville Thursday night; the writer says he confessed.

accounts.label: Columbia wire (Dec. 8 and Dec. 10)
accounts.gist: The assault took place Thursday evening; Barnett was captured twenty miles away, followed by a lynching party, landed in jail, and a second party organized afterwards but dispersed; he 'may be lynched at any moment'.

framing.detail: The Enquirer's 'AN ATROCIOUS OUTRAGE' called Barnett a 'black fiend' and 'brute' and said he 'escaped his merited punishment', yet praised the 'law abiding spirit of the Junction people'.
The New York Sun ran the Columbia dispatch as 'A Negro in Danger of Lynching', presenting the assault as fact.
The Richmond Daily Times headlined the wire 'WORK OF A NEGRO FIEND. A Lynching Threatened at Any Moment.'
